Optimal Control of the Two-Dimensional Vlasov-Maxwell System

Jörg Weber
University of Bayreuth, 95440 Bayreuth, Bavaria, Germany
Joerg.Weber@uni-bayreuth.de
Abstract

The time evolution of a collisionless plasma is modeled by the Vlasov-Maxwell system which couples the Vlasov equation (the transport equation) with the Maxwell equations of electrodynamics. We only consider a ’two-dimensional’ version of the problem since existence of global, classical solutions of the full three-dimensional problem is not known. We add external currents to the system, in applications generated by coils, to control the plasma in a proper way. After considering global existence of solutions to this system, differentiability of the control-to-state operator is proved. In applications, on the one hand, we want the shape of the plasma to be close to some desired shape. On the other hand, a cost term penalizing the external currents shall be as small as possible. These two aims lead to minimizing some objective function. We restrict ourselves to only such control currents that are realizable in applications. After that, we prove existence of a minimizer and deduce first order optimality conditions and the adjoint equation.

Keywords: relativistic Vlasov-Maxwell system, optimal control with PDE constraints, nonlinear partial differential equations, calculus of variations

MSC Classification: 49J20, 35Q61, 35Q83, 82D10.

1 Introduction

1.1 The system

The time evolution of a collisionless plasma is modeled by the Vlasov-Maxwell system. Collisions among the plasma particles can be neglected if the plasma is sufficiently rarefied or hot. The particles only interact through electromagnetic fields created collectively. We only consider plasmas consisting of just one particle species, for example, electrons. This work can immediately be adapted to the case of several particle species. For the sake of simplicity, we choose units such that physical constants like the speed of light, the charge and rest mass of an individual particle are normalized to unity. Allowing the particles to move at relativistic speeds, the three-dimensional Vlasov-Maxwell system is given by

OPEN∂tf+p^⋅∂xf+(E+p^×BCLOSE)⋅∂pf\displaystyle\partial_{t}f+\widehat{p}\cdot\partial_{x}f+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(E+\widehat{p}\times B}}\right)\cdot\partial_{p}f =0,\displaystyle=0, (1a)
∂tE−curlx⁡B\displaystyle\partial_{t}E-\curl_{x}B =−jf,\displaystyle=-j_{f}, (1b)
∂tB+curlx⁡E\displaystyle\partial_{t}B+\curl_{x}E =0,\displaystyle=0, (1c)
divx⁡E\displaystyle\divg_{x}E =ρ,\displaystyle=\rho, (1d)
divx⁡B\displaystyle\divg_{x}B =0,\displaystyle=0, (1e)
ρf\displaystyle\rho_{f} =4​π​∫f​𝑑p,\displaystyle=4\pi\int{f\,dp}, (1f)
jf\displaystyle j_{f} =4​π​∫p^​f​𝑑p.\displaystyle=4\pi\int{\widehat{p}f\,dp}. (1g)

Here, the Vlasov equation is (1a) and the Maxwell equations of electrodynamics are (1b) to (1e). Vlasov and Maxwell equations are coupled via (1f) and (1g) rendering the whole system nonlinear due to the product term OPEN(E+p^×BCLOSE)⋅∂pf\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(E+\widehat{p}\times B}}\right)\cdot\partial_{p}f. In particular, OPENf=f​(t,x,pCLOSE)f=f\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(t,x,p}}\right) denotes the density of the particles on phase space, and OPENE=E​(t,xCLOSE)E=E\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(t,x}}\right), OPENB=B​(t,xCLOSE)B=B\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(t,x}}\right) are the electromagnetic fields, whereby t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}, xx, and p∈ℝ3p\in\mathbb{R}^{3} stand for time, position in space, and momentum. The abbreviation p^=p1+|p|2\widehat{p}=\frac{p}{\sqrt{1+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|p}}\right|^{2}}} denotes the velocity of a particle with momentum pp. Furthermore, some moments of ff appear as source terms in the Maxwell equations, that is to say jfj_{f} and ρf\rho_{f} which equal the current and charge density up to the constant 4​π4\pi.

However, we have not readily explained the source term ρ\rho in (1d). If we would demand divx⁡E=ρf\divg_{x}E=\rho_{f} this would lead to a seeming contradiction: Formally integrating this equation with respect to xx (and assuming E→0E\rightarrow 0 rapidly enough at ∞\infty) leads to ∫ρf​𝑑x=0\int{\rho_{f}\,dx=0} and hence f=0f=0 by f̊≥0\mathring{f}\geq 0. This problem is caused by our simplifying restriction to one species of particles and is resolved by adding some terms to ρf\rho_{f}, for example a neutralizing background density, so that we have a total charge density ρ\rho with vanishing space integral.

Considering the Cauchy problem for the above system, we moreover demand

f(0,x,pCLOSE)=f̊(x,pCLOSE),E(0,xCLOSE)=E̊(xCLOSE),B(0,xCLOSE)=B̊(xCLOSE),\displaystyle f\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0,x,p}}\right)=\mathring{f}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p}}\right),E\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0,x}}\right)=\mathring{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),B\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0,x}}\right)=\mathring{B}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right),

where f̊≥0\mathring{f}\geq 0, E̊\mathring{E}, and B̊\mathring{B} are some given initial data.

Unfortunately, existence of global (i.e., global in time), classical (i.e., continuously differentiable) solutions for general (smooth) data is an open problem in the three-dimensional setting. It is only known that global weak solutions can be obtained. This was proved by R.J. Di Perna and P.L. Lions [1]. For a detailed insight concerning this matter we recommend the review article [17] by G. Rein. As for global existence of classical solutions, the strategy was to first consider lower dimensional settings. R. Glassey and J. Schaeffer proved global existence of classical solutions in the one and one-half [5], the two [7, 8], and the two and one-half dimensional setting [6].

Since it is convenient to have global existence of classical solutions on hand, we consider a two-dimensional version of the problem in this work. Notice that mutatis mutandis all results and techniques can be applied to the full three-dimensional setting once global existence of classical solutions has been proved. The restriction to ’two-dimensionality’ is to be understood in the following sense: All functions shall be independent of the third variables x3x_{3} and p3p_{3}. This new model describes a plasma where the particles only move in the OPEN(x1,x2CLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x_{1},x_{2}}}\right)-plane, but the plasma extends in the x3x_{3}-direction infinitely. To ensure that these properties are preserved in time, we have to demand that the electric field lies in the plane and that the magnetic field is perpendicular to the plane so that OPENE=OPEN(E1​(t,xCLOSE),E2​(t,xCLOSE),0)E=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(E_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(t,x}}\right),E_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(t,x}}\right),0}}\right) and OPENB=(0,0,B​(t,xCLOSE))B=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0,0,B\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(t,x}}\right)}}\right). Here and in the following, let OPENx=(x1,x2CLOSE)x=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x_{1},x_{2}}}\right) and OPENp=(p1,p2CLOSE)p=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p_{1},p_{2}}}\right) be two-dimensional variables. Note that hence the magnetic field is always divergence free with respect to xx, so that (1e) is always satisfied and will no longer be mentioned. The two-dimensional Vlasov-Maxwell system reads

∂tf+p^⋅∂xf+(E+(p^2,−p^1CLOSE)​B)⋅∂pf\displaystyle\partial_{t}f+\widehat{p}\cdot\partial_{x}f+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(E+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\widehat{p}_{2},-\widehat{p}_{1}}}\right)B}}\right)\cdot\partial_{p}f =0,\displaystyle=0,
∂tE1−∂x2B\displaystyle\partial_{t}E_{1}-\partial_{x_{2}}B =−jf,1,\displaystyle=-j_{f,1},
∂tE2+∂x1B\displaystyle\partial_{t}E_{2}+\partial_{x_{1}}B =−jf,2,\displaystyle=-j_{f,2},
∂tB+∂x1E2−∂x2E1\displaystyle\partial_{t}B+\partial_{x_{1}}E_{2}-\partial_{x_{2}}E_{1} =0,\displaystyle=0,
divx⁡E\displaystyle\divg_{x}E =ρ,\displaystyle=\rho,
OPEN(f,E,BCLOSE)|t=0\displaystyle\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left.\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f,E,B}}\right)}}\right|_{t=0} OPEN=(f̊,E̊,B̊CLOSE).\displaystyle=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathring{f},\mathring{E},\mathring{B}}}\right).

The goal is to control the plasma in a proper way. Thereto we add external currents UU to the system, in applications generated by electric coils. These currents, like the electric field and the current density of the plasma particles, have to lie in the plane and have to be independent of the third space coordinate. Of course, there will be an external charge density ρext\rho_{\mathrm{ext}} corresponding to the external current. It is natural to assume local conservation of the external charge, i.e.

∂tρext+divx⁡U=0.\displaystyle\partial_{t}\rho_{\mathrm{ext}}+\divg_{x}U=0.

Hence we can eliminate ρext\rho_{\mathrm{ext}} via

ρext=ρ̊ext−∫0tdivx⁡U​𝑑τ.\displaystyle\rho_{\mathrm{ext}}=\mathring{\rho}_{\mathrm{ext}}-\int_{0}^{t}{\divg_{x}U\,d\tau}.

The initial value ρ̊ext\mathring{\rho}_{\mathrm{ext}} will be added to the background density. This total background density will be neglected throughout this work.

Also, for simplicity, we do not consider material parameters, for example for modeling supraconductors in a fusion reactor, that is to say permittivity and permeability, which would appear in the Maxwell equations.

In the following, we consider the controlled relativistic Vlasov-Maxwell system

OPEN∂tf+p^⋅∂xf+(E−p^⊥​BCLOSE)⋅∂pf=0,∂tE1−∂x2B=−jf,1−U1,∂tE2+∂x1B=−jf,2−U2,∂tB+∂x1E2−∂x2E1=0,divx⁡E=ρf−∫0tdivx⁡U​dτ,OPEN(f,E,BCLOSE)|t=0OPEN=(f̊,E̊,B̊CLOSE)}\displaystyle\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left.\begin{aligned} \partial_{t}f+\widehat{p}\cdot\partial_{x}f+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(E-\widehat{p}^{\bot}B}}\right)\cdot\partial_{p}f&=0,\\ \partial_{t}E_{1}-\partial_{x_{2}}B&=-j_{f,1}-U_{1},\\ \partial_{t}E_{2}+\partial_{x_{1}}B&=-j_{f,2}-U_{2},\\ \partial_{t}B+\partial_{x_{1}}E_{2}-\partial_{x_{2}}E_{1}&=0,\\ \divg_{x}E&=\rho_{f}-\int_{0}^{t}{\divg_{x}U\,d\tau},\\ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left.\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f,E,B}}\right)}}\right|_{t=0}&=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathring{f},\mathring{E},\mathring{B}}}\right)\end{aligned}}}\right\} (CVM)

on a finite time interval [0,TCLOSE]\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[0,T}}\right] with given T>0T>0; here we introduced the abbreviation OPENa⊥=(−a2,a1CLOSE)a^{\bot}=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(-a_{2},a_{1}}}\right) for a∈ℝ2a\in\mathbb{R}^{2}.

It is well known that LqL^{q}-norms (with respect to OPEN(x,pCLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p}}\right), 1≤q≤∞1\leq q\leq\infty) of ff are preserved in time by ff solving the Vlasov equation since the vector field OPEN(p^,E−p^⊥​BCLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\widehat{p},E-\widehat{p}^{\bot}B}}\right) is divergence free in OPEN(x,pCLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x,p}}\right). Therefore, especially, the L1L^{1}-norm (with respect to xx) of the charge density ρf\rho_{f} is constant in time.

The outline of our work is the following: In the first part, we have to prove unique solvability of (CVM). Of course, some regularity assumptions on the external current and the initial data have to be made in order to prove existence of classical solutions. In the second part, we consider an optimal control problem. On the one hand, we want the shape of the plasma to be close to some desired shape. On the other hand, the external currents shall be as small as possible. These two aims lead to minimizing some objective function. To analyze the optimal control problem, it is convenient to show differentiability of the control-to-state operator first. After that, we prove existence of a minimizer and deduce first order optimality conditions and the adjoint equation.

The steps mentioned above were carried out by P. Knopf [13] and, only considering realizable control fields, by Knopf and the author [14] for the three-dimensional Vlasov-Poisson system with an external magnetic field. The consideration of the latter setting has the advantage of being able to work in three dimensions, but has the disadvantage of only imposing Poisson’s equation, that is, Maxwell’s equations with an internal magnetic field sufficiently small to be neglected, for the electromagnetic fields, which make things easier due to the elliptic nature of Poisson’s equation in contrast to the hyperbolic nature of the (time evolutionary) Maxwell equations.

Also other approaches for controlling a Vlasov-Maxwell plasma have been considered in the literature, but they are different in nature compared to our approach. We refer to [3, 16] and the references therein.

1.3 Maxwell equations

We will have to consider first order and second order Maxwell equations. It is well known that they are equivalent and that the divergence equations propagate in time if local conservation of charge holds, i.e.

∂tρ+divx⁡j=0.\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \partial_{t}\rho+\divg_{x}j=0.\end{aligned} (LC)

In our two-dimensional setting with fields OPEN(E1,E2,0CLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(E_{1},E_{2},0}}\right) and OPEN(0,0,BCLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0,0,B}}\right) we conclude:

Lemma 2.

Let E̊\mathring{E} and B̊\mathring{B} be of class C2C^{2} and EE, B∈C2B\in C^{2}, and ρ\rho, j∈C1j\in C^{1}. If the conditions

OPENdiv⁡E̊=ρ​(0CLOSE)\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \divg\mathring{E}=\rho\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0}}\right)\end{aligned} (CC)

and

∂tρ+divx⁡j=0\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \partial_{t}\rho+\divg_{x}j=0\end{aligned} (LC)

First, OPEN∂t(−∫0tdivxddτ)+divx⁡d=0\partial_{t}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(-\int_{0}^{t}{\divg_{x}d\,d\tau}}}\right)+\divg_{x}d=0 is obvious. Furthermore, integrating the Vlasov equation with respect to pp instantly yields ∂tρf+divx⁡jf=0\partial_{t}\rho_{f}+\divg_{x}j_{f}=0. ∎

2 Existence results

2.1 Estimates on the fields

2.1.1 A generalized system

The most important tool to get certain bounds is to have representations of the fields. One can use the solution formula for the wave equation and after some transformation of the integral expressions Gronwall-like estimates on the density and the fields can be derived. These bounds, for instance, will imply that the sequences constructed in Section 2.3 converge in a certain sense. Having that in mind it is useful not to work with the system (CVM) but with a somewhat generalized one with second order Maxwell equations:

OPEN∂tf+p^⋅∂xf+α⁡(pCLOSE)​K⋅∂pf=g,∂t2E−Δ​E=−∂tjf−∂td−∂xρf+∂x∫0tdivxddτ,∂t2B−Δ​B=∂x1jf,2−∂x2jf,1+∂x1d2−∂x2d1,OPENOPEN(f,E,BCLOSE)​(0CLOSE)OPEN=(f̊,E̊,B̊CLOSE),OPEN∂tE​(0CLOSE)OPENOPEN=(∂x2B̊,−∂x1B̊)−jf̊−d⁡(0CLOSE),OPEN∂tB​(0CLOSE)=−∂x1E̊2+∂x2E̊1,}\displaystyle\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left.\begin{aligned} \partial_{t}f+\widehat{p}\cdot\partial_{x}f+\alpha\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(p}}\right)K\cdot\partial_{p}f&=g,\\ \partial_{t}^{2}E-\Delta E&=-\partial_{t}j_{f}-\partial_{t}d-\partial_{x}\rho_{f}+\partial_{x}\int_{0}^{t}{\divg_{x}d\,d\tau},\\ \partial_{t}^{2}B-\Delta B&=\partial_{x_{1}}j_{f,2}-\partial_{x_{2}}j_{f,1}+\partial_{x_{1}}d_{2}-\partial_{x_{2}}d_{1},\\ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f,E,B}}\right)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0}}\right)&=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathring{f},\mathring{E},\mathring{B}}}\right),\\ \partial_{t}E\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0}}\right)&=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\partial_{x_{2}}\mathring{B},-\partial_{x_{1}}\mathring{B}}}\right)-j_{\mathring{f}}-d\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0}}\right),\\ \partial_{t}B\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0}}\right)&=-\partial_{x_{1}}\mathring{E}_{2}+\partial_{x_{2}}\mathring{E}_{1},\end{aligned}}}\right\} (GVM)

Proof.

The representation formula are derived in much the same way as in [7, Thm. 1]. The only difference is that here the source terms gg and dd appear. The support assertion is an immediate consequence of the representation formula. Physically, this is a result of the fact that electromagnetic fields can not propagate faster than the speed of light. The estimates on the SS-and TT-terms are derived in much the same way as in [8, Sec. 2]. Note that the energy estimates of Lemma 8, that had to be modified in our situation, are enough to carry out the the proofs therein.

The estimate on the DD-terms is derived straightforwardly, as well as the estimate on E0E^{0}, B0B^{0}, the latter parts only containing terms of the initial data and OPENU​(0CLOSE)U\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0}}\right). ∎

Now we can finally prove:

2.3 Existence of classical solutions

2.3.2 Uniqueness

We prove uniqueness of the solution.

Theorem 13.

The obtained solution 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁(f,E,B𝐶𝐿𝑂𝑆𝐸)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f,E,B}}\right) of (CVM) is unique in 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁C1×(C2𝐶𝐿𝑂𝑆𝐸)2C^{1}\times\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(C^{2}}}\right)^{2}.

Proof.

The proof is standard. Consider the difference of two solutions and apply Lemmas 4 and 5 to show that the difference vanishes after a Gronwall argument. ∎

4 Optimal control problem

Now we consider some optimal control problems. We want to minimize some objective function that depends on the external control UU and the state OPEN(f,E,BCLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f,E,B}}\right). The control and the state are coupled via (CVM) so that (CVM) appears as a constraint.

We first give thought to a problem with general controls and a general objective function. Then we proceed with optimizing problems where the objective function is explicitly given and where the control set is restricted to such controls that are realizable in applications concerning the control of a plasma.

4.1 General problem

4.1.1 Control space

Until now we have worked with the control space

V={U∈W2,1(0,T,Cb4​(ℝ2;ℝ2CLOSE))∣U(t,xCLOSE)=0 for |x|≥L}.\displaystyle V=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{U\in W^{2,1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0,T;C_{b}^{4}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathbb{R}^{2};\mathbb{R}^{2}}}\right)}}\right)\mid U\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(t,x}}\right)=0\text{ for }\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|x}}\right|\geq L}}\right\}.

To apply standard optimization techniques it is necessary that the control space is reflexive. Hence we choose

𝒰:={U∈H2(0,T,W5,γ​(ℝ2;ℝ2CLOSE))∣U(t,xCLOSE)=0 for |x|≥L},\displaystyle\mathcal{U}:=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{U\in H^{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0,T;W^{5,\gamma}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathbb{R}^{2};\mathbb{R}^{2}}}\right)}}\right)\mid U\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(t,x}}\right)=0\text{ for }\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|x}}\right|\geq L}}\right\},

where γ>2\gamma>2 is fixed, equipped with the OPENH2​(0,T;W5,γCLOSE)H^{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0,T;W^{5,\gamma}}}\right)-norm. By Sobolev’s embedding theorems, 𝒰\mathcal{U} is continuously embedded in VV.

In accordance with Theorems 12 and 17, we have already proved that there is a continuously differentiable control-to-state operator

S:V\displaystyle S\colon V OPEN→(Cb2([0,TCLOSE]×ℝ4)×Cb2([0,TCLOSE]×ℝ2;ℝ2)×Cb2([0,TCLOSE]×ℝ2),‖⋅‖OPENC​(0,T;L2CLOSE)),\displaystyle\rightarrow\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(C_{b}^{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[0,T}}\right]\times\mathbb{R}^{4}}}\right)\times C_{b}^{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[0,T}}\right]\times\mathbb{R}^{2};\mathbb{R}^{2}}}\right)\times C_{b}^{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[0,T}}\right]\times\mathbb{R}^{2}}}\right),\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|\cdot}}\right\|_{C\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0,T;L^{2}}}\right)}}}\right),
U\displaystyle U OPEN↦(f,E,BCLOSE),\displaystyle\mapsto\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f,E,B}}\right),

such that (CVM) holds for OPEN(f,E,BCLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f,E,B}}\right) and control UU. Furthermore, the map U↦ρfU\mapsto\rho_{f} is continuously differentiable with respect to the OPENC​(0,T;L2CLOSE)C\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0,T;L^{2}}}\right)- and OPENC​(0,T;L1CLOSE)C\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0,T;L^{1}}}\right)-norm in the image space. Moreover, the Cb2C_{b}^{2}-norm and the xx- and pp-support of OPEN(f,E,BCLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f,E,B}}\right) are controlled by a constant only depending on TT, LL, the initial data, and ‖U‖V\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|U}}\right\|_{V}.

By 𝒰↪V\mathcal{U}\hookrightarrow V, these assertions also hold with 𝒰\mathcal{U} instead of VV.

4.1.2 Existence of minimizers

We consider the general problem

minOPENOPEN(f,E,BCLOSE)∈(C2∩H1CLOSE)3,U∈𝒰OPENϕ​(f,E,B,UCLOSE)s.t.OPENOPEN(f,E,BCLOSE)=S​(UCLOSE).}\displaystyle\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left.\begin{aligned} \min_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f,E,B}}\right)\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(C^{2}\cap H^{1}}}\right)^{3},U\in\mathcal{U}\end{subarray}}\,&\phi\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f,E,B,U}}\right)\\ \text{s.t.}\,&\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f,E,B}}\right)=S\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U}}\right).\end{aligned}}}\right\} (GP)

We have to specify some assumptions on ϕ\phi:

Condition 18.
\hyper@anchor
  1. i)

    ϕ:(C2∩H1CLOSE)3×𝒰→ℝ∪{∞}\phi\colon\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(C^{2}\cap H^{1}}}\right)^{3}\times\mathcal{U}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\cup\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\infty}}\right\} and ϕ≢∞\phi\not\equiv\infty,

  2. ii)

    ϕ\phi is coercive in U∈𝒰U\in\mathcal{U}, i.e. in general: Let XX, YY be normed spaces; ψ:X×Y→ℝ\psi\colon X\times Y\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is said to be coercive in y∈Yy\in Y iff for all sequences OPEN(ykCLOSE)⊂Y\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(y_{k}}}\right)\subset Y with ‖yk‖Y→∞\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|y_{k}}}\right\|_{Y}\rightarrow\infty, k→∞k\rightarrow\infty, then also OPENψ​(xk,ykCLOSE)→∞\psi\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x_{k},y_{k}}}\right)\rightarrow\infty, k→∞k\rightarrow\infty, for any sequence OPEN(xkCLOSE)⊂X\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x_{k}}}\right)\subset X,

  3. iii)

    ϕ\phi is weakly lower semicontinuous, i.e.: if OPENOPEN(fk,Ek,BkCLOSE)⇀(f,E,BCLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f_{k},E_{k},B_{k}}}\right)\rightharpoonup\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f,E,B}}\right) in H1H^{1} and Uk⇀UU_{k}\rightharpoonup U in 𝒰\mathcal{U}, then OPENOPENϕ⁡(f,E,B,UCLOSE)≤lim infk→∞ϕ⁡(fk,Ek,Bk,UkCLOSE)\phi\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f,E,B,U}}\right)\leq\liminf_{\begin{subarray}{c}k\rightarrow\infty\end{subarray}}\phi\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f_{k},E_{k},B_{k},U_{k}}}\right).

These assumptions allow us to prove existence of a (not necessarily unique) minimizer. We will first prove a lemma that will be useful later:

Lemma 19.

Let 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁(Uk𝐶𝐿𝑂𝑆𝐸)⊂V\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U_{k}}}\right)\subset V be bounded and 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁(fk,Ek,Bk𝐶𝐿𝑂𝑆𝐸)=S​(Uk𝐶𝐿𝑂𝑆𝐸)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f_{k},E_{k},B_{k}}}\right)=S\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U_{k}}}\right). Then, after extracting a suitable subsequence, it holds that:

  1. i)

    The sequences OPEN(fkCLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f_{k}}}\right), OPEN(EkCLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(E_{k}}}\right), and OPEN(BkCLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(B_{k}}}\right) converge weakly in H1H^{1}, weakly-* in W1,∞W^{1,\infty}, and strongly in L2L^{2} to some ff, EE, and BB.

  2. ii)

    There is r>0r>0 such that ff, EE, BB, and, for all k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, fkf_{k}, EkE_{k}, and BkB_{k} vanish if |x|≥r\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|x}}\right|\geq r or |p|≥r\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|p}}\right|\geq r.

  3. iii)

    If additionally Uk→UU_{k}\rightarrow U in the sense of distributions for some U∈VU\in V for k→∞k\rightarrow\infty, then OPENOPEN(f,E,BCLOSE)=S​(UCLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f,E,B}}\right)=S\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U}}\right) and ff, EE, and BB are of class Cb2C_{b}^{2}.

Proof.

By Theorem 12, on the one hand, OPEN(fk,Ek,BkCLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f_{k},E_{k},B_{k}}}\right) is bounded in the Cb1C_{b}^{1}-norm. On the other hand, fkf_{k} vanishes as soon as |p|\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|p}}\right| is large enough uniformly in kk. Moreover, fkf_{k}, EkE_{k}, and BkB_{k} vanish as soon as |x|\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|x}}\right| is large enough. Hence OPEN(fk,Ek,BkCLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f_{k},E_{k},B_{k}}}\right) is also bounded in H1H^{1} and in OPENH1​(0,T;L2CLOSE)H^{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0,T;L^{2}}}\right). Together with the boundedness in Cb1C_{b}^{1}, OPEN(fk,Ek,BkCLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f_{k},E_{k},B_{k}}}\right) converge, after extracting a suitable subsequence, to some OPEN(f,E,BCLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f,E,B}}\right), namely weakly in H1H^{1}, and weakly-* in W1,∞W^{1,\infty}. This proves ii) and part of i).

For the remaining part of i) (strong convergence in L2L^{2}) we have to exploit some compactness. This compactness is guaranteed by the theorem of Rellich-Kondrachov. By the reasoning above, OPEN(fk,Ek,BkCLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f_{k},E_{k},B_{k}}}\right) are bounded in H1H^{1} and in fact, only a bounded subset of the xx- and pp-space matters. Hence (a subsequence of) OPEN(fk,Ek,BkCLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f_{k},E_{k},B_{k}}}\right) converges strongly in L2L^{2} to the limit OPEN(f,E,BCLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f,E,B}}\right).

For iii), we have to pass to the limit in (CVM). First, the initial conditions are preserved in the limit since OPENOPENH1↪H1​(0,T;L2CLOSE)↪C⁡(0,T;L2CLOSE)H^{1}\hookrightarrow H^{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0,T;L^{2}}}\right)\hookrightarrow C\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0,T;L^{2}}}\right). Furthermore the Vlasov and Maxwell equations hold pointwise almost everywhere for the limit functions: The only difficult part is the nonlinear term in the Vlasov equation. To handle this, we have to make use of the strong convergence in L2L^{2} obtained above. We find for each OPENφ∈Cc∞​(]0,T[×ℝ4)\varphi\in C_{c}^{\infty}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left]0,T}}\right[\times\mathbb{R}^{4}}}\right) that

≤|∫0T∫∫(E−p^⊥​BCLOSE)⋅(∂pfk−∂pfCLOSE)φdpdxdt|\displaystyle\leq\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|\int_{0}^{T}{\int{\int{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(E-\widehat{p}^{\bot}B}}\right)\cdot\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\partial_{p}f_{k}-\partial_{p}f}}\right)\varphi\,dp}dx}dt}}}\right|
+‖∂pfk‖∞∫0T∫∫(|Ek−E|+|Bk−B|)|φ|dpdxdt.\displaystyle\phantom{=\ }+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|\partial_{p}f_{k}}}\right\|_{\infty}\int_{0}^{T}{\int{\int{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|E_{k}-E}}\right|+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|B_{k}-B}}\right|}}\right)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|\varphi}}\right|dp}dx}dt}.

Both terms converge to 00 for k→∞k\rightarrow\infty since fk⇀ff_{k}\rightharpoonup f in H1H^{1}, Ek→EE_{k}\rightarrow E, Bk→BB_{k}\rightarrow B in L2L^{2}, and fkf_{k} is bounded in Cb1C_{b}^{1}. Therefore, altogether, (CVM) holds pointwise almost everywhere. Now we can apply Theorem 14 to conclude OPEN(f,E,BCLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f,E,B}}\right) equals OPENS​(UCLOSE)S\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U}}\right) and is hence of class Cb2C_{b}^{2}. ∎

Theorem 20.

Let ϕ\phi satisfy Condition 18. Then there is a minimizer of (GP).

Proof.

We consider a minimizing sequence OPEN(fk,Ek,Bk,UkCLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f_{k},E_{k},B_{k},U_{k}}}\right) with OPENOPEN(fk,Ek,BkCLOSE)=S​(UkCLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f_{k},E_{k},B_{k}}}\right)=S\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U_{k}}}\right) and

limk→∞ϕ(fk,Ek,Bk,UkCLOSE)=m:=infOPENOPENU∈𝒰,(f,E,BCLOSE)=S⁡(UCLOSE)ϕ(f,E,B,UCLOSE)∈ℝ∪{−∞}.\displaystyle\lim_{\begin{subarray}{c}k\rightarrow\infty\end{subarray}}\phi\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f_{k},E_{k},B_{k},U_{k}}}\right)=m:=\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}U\in\mathcal{U},\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f,E,B}}\right)=S\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U}}\right)\end{subarray}}\phi\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f,E,B,U}}\right)\in\mathbb{R}\cup\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{-\infty}}\right\}.

By coercivity in UU, cf. Condition 18 ii), OPEN(UkCLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U_{k}}}\right) is bounded in 𝒰\mathcal{U} and therefore in VV. Hence we may extract a weakly convergent subsequence (also denoted by UkU_{k}) since OPENH2​(0,T;W5,γCLOSE)H^{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0,T;W^{5,\gamma}}}\right) is reflexive. The weak limit UU is the candidate for being an optimal control. Of course, by weak convergence, UU vanishes for |x|≥L\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|x}}\right|\geq L; hence U∈𝒰U\in\mathcal{U}. Because of 𝒰↪L1\mathcal{U}\hookrightarrow L^{1} we also get Uk⇀UU_{k}\rightharpoonup U in L1L^{1} and hence Uk→UU_{k}\rightarrow U in the sense of distributions. Lemma 19 yields OPENOPEN(fk,Ek,BkCLOSE)⇀(f,E,BCLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f_{k},E_{k},B_{k}}}\right)\rightharpoonup\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f,E,B}}\right) in H1H^{1} (after extracting a suitable subsequence) and OPENOPEN(f,E,BCLOSE)=S​(UCLOSE)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f,E,B}}\right)=S\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U}}\right). Together with the weak lower semicontinuity of ϕ\phi, see Condition 18 iii), we instantly get OPENϕ​(f,E,B,UCLOSE)=m\phi\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f,E,B,U}}\right)=m which proves optimality. ∎

In order to be able of examining some problem that is somehow application-oriented, we first have to think about possible problems concerning the conditions on the objective function ϕ\phi. Especially the coercivity in UU will make some trouble since the 𝒰\mathcal{U}-norm is pretty strong. One can try to guarantee these conditions in various ways, for example if ϕ(f,E,B,UCLOSE)=ψ(f,E,BCLOSE)+‖U‖𝒰2\phi\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f,E,B,U}}\right)=\psi\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f,E,B}}\right)+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|U}}\right\|_{\mathcal{U}}^{2}; the objective function contains some cost term of the control in the full 𝒰\mathcal{U}-norm. But typically in applications, such a strong cost term makes no sense. Furthermore, first order optimality conditions would contain a differential equation of very high order, which is hard to solve.

On the other hand, we can not simply use a less regular control space. Firstly, we need 𝒰↪V\mathcal{U}\hookrightarrow V to ensure that the control-to-state operator is differentiable; this will be useful later. Secondly, 𝒰\mathcal{U} needs to be reflexive to extract (in some sense) converging subsequences from a minimizing sequence. Here we should remark that we also could demand W2,pW^{2,p}-regularity in time for p>1p>1 instead of H2H^{2}-regularity which would allow more controls if 1<p<21<p<2. However, working in a H2H^{2}-setting (at least in time) is more convenient.

4.2 An optimization problem with realizable external currents

4.2.1 Motivation

As the previous considerations suggest, it would be nice if we somehow eliminated the variability of the control with respect to the space coordinate. This can be achieved by only considering controls of the form

U(t,xCLOSE)=∑j=1Nuj(tCLOSE)zj(xCLOSE)\displaystyle U\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(t,x}}\right)=\sum_{j=1}^{N}{u_{j}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(t}}\right)z_{j}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x}}\right)}

where the functions OPEN0≢zj∈Cb6​(ℝ2;ℝ2CLOSE)0\not\equiv z_{j}\in C_{b}^{6}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathbb{R}^{2};\mathbb{R}^{2}}}\right) with zjz_{j} vanishing for |x|≥rj>0\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|x}}\right|\geq r_{j}>0 are fixed and we only vary the functions OPENuj∈H2​([0,TCLOSE])u_{j}\in H^{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[0,T}}\right]}}\right).

From a physical point of view, this model describes an ensemble of NN coils with ’size’ rjr_{j}, that stay fixed in time. Obviously, UU is an element of VV if we set L=max{rj∣j=1,…N}L=\max\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{r_{j}\mid j=1,\dots N}}\right\}. Each coil generates a current zjz_{j} at full capacity that is tangential to the plane and that extends infinitely in the third space dimension. We control the system by turning these coils on whereby the capacity uju_{j} is suitably adjusted as a function of time. Hence we will have to consider an additional constraint |uj|≤1\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|u_{j}}}\right|\leq 1. Physically, the consideration only of controls of the above form is no substantial restriction at all because only such control fields are realizable in applications.

A similar approach was done by P. Knopf and the author [14].

4.2.2 Formulation

The problem to be considered is the following:

min(f,E,BCLOSE)∈(C2∩H1CLOSE)3,u∈H2([0,TCLOSE])N12‖ρf−ρd‖OPENL2​([0,TCLOSE]×ℝ2)2+β2∑j=1Ncj(‖uj‖OPENL2​([0,TCLOSE])2OPEN+β1‖∂tuj‖OPENL2​([0,TCLOSE])2+β2‖∂t2uj‖OPENL2​([0,TCLOSE])2)s.t.(f,E,BCLOSE)=S(∑j=1Nuj​zjCLOSE),|uj|≤1}\displaystyle\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left.\begin{aligned} \min_{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f,E,B}}\right)\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(C^{2}\cap H^{1}}}\right)^{3},u\in H^{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[0,T}}\right]}}\right)^{N}}\,&\frac{1}{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|\rho_{f}-\rho_{d}}}\right\|_{L^{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[0,T}}\right]\times\mathbb{R}^{2}}}\right)}^{2}+\frac{\beta}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{N}{c_{j}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|u_{j}}}\right\|_{L^{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[0,T}}\right]}}\right)}^{2}}}\right.}\\ &\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left.+\beta_{1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|\partial_{t}u_{j}}}\right\|_{L^{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[0,T}}\right]}}\right)}^{2}+\beta_{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|\partial_{t}^{2}u_{j}}}\right\|_{L^{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[0,T}}\right]}}\right)}^{2}}}\right)\\ \text{s.t.}\,&\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f,E,B}}\right)=S\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\sum_{j=1}^{N}{u_{j}z_{j}}}}\right),\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|u_{j}}}\right|\leq 1\end{aligned}}}\right\} (P)

where cj:=‖zj‖OPENL2​(ℝ2;ℝ2CLOSE)2c_{j}:=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|z_{j}}}\right\|_{L^{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathbb{R}^{2};\mathbb{R}^{2}}}\right)}^{2}. We give some comments on the objective function:

  • •

    The charge density shall be as close as possible to some given desired density OPENOPENρd=ρd​(t,xCLOSE)∈L2​([0,TCLOSE]×ℝ2)\rho_{d}=\rho_{d}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(t,x}}\right)\in L^{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[0,T}}\right]\times\mathbb{R}^{2}}}\right). One could consider the L2L^{2}-norm of some f−fdf-f_{d} instead but the space coordinates of the particles are of actual interest rather than their momenta.

  • •

    Furthermore, the cost term containing the control shall be as small as possible. We have to use the full H2H^{2}-norm (an equivalent norm, to be more precise) of the uju_{j} in the regularization term so that the objective function is coercive in OPENu∈H2​([0,TCLOSE])Nu\in H^{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[0,T}}\right]}}\right)^{N}. However, the L2L^{2}-norms of the uju_{j} itself are more interesting than the ones of their derivatives. Hence it is suitable to choose 0<β1,β2≪10<\beta_{1},\beta_{2}\ll 1.

  • •

    The parameter β>0\beta>0 indicates which of the two aims mentioned above shall rather be achieved.

System (Ad) has to be investigated. It is a final value problem which can easily be turned into an initial value problem via OPENOPENg~​(t,x,pCLOSE)=g​(T−t,−x,−pCLOSE)\widetilde{g}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(t,x,p}}\right)=g\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(T-t,-x,-p}}\right) and OPENOPENh~​(t,xCLOSE)=h​(T−t,−xCLOSE)\widetilde{h}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(t,x}}\right)=h\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(T-t,-x}}\right), so that the left hand sides of the differential equations in (Ad) do not change. In other words, the hyperbolic system (Ad) is time reversible.

To show unique solvability of (Ad), one can proceed similar to the dealing with (LVM). Yet there are some differences, which we will briefly sketch. Firstly, the source terms in the Maxwell equations are not the current densities induced by gg but some other moments of gg. Additionally, even in the fourth equation of (Ad) a source term appears. Hence we have to prove analogues of Lemmas 5 and 7 with more general source terms. Secondly, the right hand side of the Vlasov equation (and hence a solution gg) does not have compact support with respect to pp. But this will not cause any problems since in a representation formula for hh there will appear a factor ∂pf\partial_{p}f (or first derivatives of ∂pf\partial_{p}f). Because of the known fact that ff is compactly supported with respect to pp uniformly in tt, xx, we do not have to demand that gg has this property. In Section 2.1 we had to assume this property for the density since the integral defining the current density induced by this density contains the factor p^\widehat{p} which is obviously not compactly supported in pp.
